titulo: The Illusion of a Stagnant Exchange Rate
resumo: USD/BRL ended four years almost exactly where it started, but that is a nominal measure, and nominal is where currency illusions settle.
corpo:
USD/BRL ended four years almost exactly where it started, but that is a nominal measure, and nominal is where currency illusions settle.

The Easy Reading

The most repeated assessment of the real over the past four years is that it has not moved. In September 2022 the dollar hovered around 5.17, and in September 2026 it is near 5.11. Between those two points, there was a range from 4.59 to 6.29 and a net balance close to zero. Range and balance, however, are different things: from the low to the high is about 37%, so the real was anything but stable, it just ended up near where it started. The conclusion that sticks is the one about the balance: the exchange rate stood still. The problem is that this conclusion is nominal, and nominal is the surface where currency illusions settle, because it treats as stable something that was only stable on the screen, ignoring that the purchasing power behind each currency moved considerably over the same interval.

Every Currency Has Two Prices

A currency has a nominal price, which is the quote, and a real price, which is that quote adjusted for the inflation differential between the two countries. The mechanism is direct. If Brazil has higher inflation than the United States and the nominal exchange rate does not move, the Brazilian currency is becoming more expensive in real terms, because the same basket of goods costs more here while the quote on the screen does not reflect that difference. A stable nominal exchange rate coexisting with higher domestic inflation is not a neutral exchange rate. It is a real appreciation disguised as stability, and that disguise is what the spot reading fails to undo.

The Real Math

There is a direct way to measure the illusion: purchasing power parity. If the exchange rate had simply tracked the inflation differential, the dollar that was worth about 5.17 in September 2022 would be near 5.49 today, because Brazil accumulated 19.8% inflation against 12.9% in the United States, and an exchange rate that merely passed through that nearly seven-point difference would be more depreciated. The dollar did not go to 5.49. It stayed near 5.11. That mechanical depreciation never came, and a stagnant nominal exchange rate, in this context, is a real appreciation of the real on the order of 7% relative to what parity would imply. The caveat is that parity is a long-term anchor, not a price the market needs to hit within four years, and deviations of this magnitude are common and correct slowly. But the direction is unambiguous: in purchasing power terms, the real that no one saw move became more expensive.

Three Scenarios for the Same Exchange Rate

A nominal balance near zero is not the absence of forces. It is the meeting of forces that pulled in opposite directions and nearly canceled each other out, and the best way to see this is to break the exchange rate down into three lenses. Parity gives the long-term equilibrium. The interest rate differential gives the effect of monetary policy. And the decomposition of the observed movement separates what came from outside from what came from inside.

It is the third lens that organizes the story. Breaking down the real's daily movement into a global dollar factor and an emerging-market currency factor, the period had two external tailwinds: the broad dollar weakened about 9%, in an environment of greater global tolerance for a weak dollar, and the emerging-market basket rose about 19%. Isolating just these external factors, the dollar should have fallen to near 4.59, a significant appreciation of the real. Isolating just what remains, the domestic component, the dollar would have gone to near 5.76. The observed figure, 5.11, is the middle ground. The external side offered Brazil a substantial appreciation, and a domestic factor gave back almost all of that gain.

This domestic component is the point where statistics end and interpretation begins. The model isolates a factor that is neither dollar nor emerging markets, and its size over the period is consistent with the fiscal deterioration of these years. That is the most plausible interpretation, not a regression output: what the model measures is a Brazilian residual, and the line of candidates to explain it, fiscal at the front, is an argument from someone reading the country, not a number the decomposition delivers ready-made. And there is a force that reinforces this reading rather than weakening it. The period saw record trade surpluses in Brazil, a tailwind that strengthens the real. The bulk of that effect, the global commodity cycle, is already captured in the peer factor, all commodity exporters, and what remains for the residual is only Brazil's specific surplus beyond its peers, which enters with a sign opposite to that of the risk premium. Even that favorable share was not enough: the domestic component outweighed it. The weight that held the currency down had to overcome not only the external tailwind but also the idiosyncratic piece of trade flow, and it still prevailed. With that caveat, the sentence that sums up the period holds: the dollar lost strength globally, which should have delivered Brazil a significant appreciation, and Brazil did not capture that appreciation because the domestic side weighed in the opposite direction.

What the Spot Rate Does Not Show: Carry

Saying Brazil gained nothing would be wrong, and this is where the math needs precision. What the real failed to capture was the currency appreciation that the external scenario offered. But staying long the real paid off, and paid off handsomely. The interest rate differential between the Selic and the Fed Funds rate yielded, cumulatively, about 43% over four years, close to 9% per year. Added to the spot movement, the total return of a position long in real and funded in dollars was approximately 45% in dollar terms, which is what the global investor actually pockets. Here is the articulation, and I separate what is fact from what is interpretation. The 43% carry is fact. Reading it as the price the market charged, up front, to carry Brazilian risk, the same domestic risk that kept the spot rate from appreciating, is a hypothesis, consistent with the data. The investor was paid precisely to take on the risk that, in the spot exchange rate, showed up as a drag. Net, the payment outweighed the drag.

It is worth being precise about the role of interest rates, because they work in both directions. In the short run, a large differential attracts capital and tends to strengthen the real, which is why the real is a classic carry currency. But that same differential is the price of a risk. The country pays one of the highest real interest rates in the world because financing its own currency is expensive, and uncovered interest rate parity posits that the high-yielding currency tends to depreciate to give back the gain from the differential. It is the systematic empirical failure of that condition that allows carry to exist and be profitable, the same carry I measured at 43%. The interest rate is, at once, the magnet that sustains the real and the price of the risk that threatens it. What the spot rate failed to capture shows up here, in the rate, and carry is the face of that price that the investor actually pockets.

Where the Reading Stops Holding

Separating what is structural from what is of the moment is what distinguishes analysis from narrative. Extending the sample to thirteen years and running the model on a rolling three-year window, the real's beta against the emerging-market peer basket stays between 0.7 and 1.1 throughout the period, spanning the 2015-2016 crisis, the pandemic, and the tightening cycle, with the confidence band never touching zero. That is structural: the real is, reliably and under any regime, a high-beta asset within the emerging market and commodity currency complex. What is not structural is the size of the domestic component. That term ranges from minus 13% to plus 9% depending on the window, with the uncertainty crossing zero almost all the time. There is a Brazil factor, but it does not have a stable number, and that is why the fiscal reading is an argument, not a measurement. Pinning down a fair price for the dollar from it would be selling a precision the data does not deliver, and the 7% real appreciation itself depends on the window and the base chosen.

The Risk That Remained

What remains is to name the risk that held the currency back, and here external data help separate two things that are usually treated as one. Brazil's five-year CDS fell from 261 to 121 basis points over the period. The price the world charges to protect against a sovereign default in dollars improved, and improved along with the emerging-market cycle. If Brazil risk were entirely there, the real would have tracked its peers. It did not. The risk that weighed is not dollar credit risk, which declined. It is the premium demanded to carry the local currency, and that shows up elsewhere. It shows up in the real interest rate, which kept Brazil among the highest in the world in 2026: even after the Copom cut the Selic rate to 13.75% in September, with inflation just below 4.5%, the ex-ante real interest rate stays near 9% (Central Bank and InfoMoney, September 2026). It shows up in the debt trajectory. General government gross debt reached 82.5% of GDP in July 2026 by the Central Bank's methodology, and the International Monetary Fund, which uses a broader definition, projects 97.8% for the year and warns that, without firmer fiscal effort, it is heading toward near 106% by 2035, raising the risk premium and the cost of financing the debt (BCB, DBGG series; IMF, Article IV Consultation, July 2026).

This is the most plausible reading of the domestic component the model isolates. The Brazilian residual is neither dollar nor emerging markets, and the leading candidate to explain it is the fiscal deterioration these same sources describe: expansionary public spending neutralizing restrictive monetary policy, with the market treating fiscal developments as more decisive for the real than the interest rate decision itself (Commerzbank, September 2026). The model does not pin down the size of this factor, and the previous section shows why: in a rolling window it has no stable number. What it delivers is direction, and the direction is consistent. The real failed to capture the appreciation that a weak dollar and strong peers offered because the domestic risk premium, fiscal at its root, moved in the opposite direction and consumed the external relief.

And yet staying long the real paid off. The same risk that kept the spot rate from appreciating was compensated, up front, with nearly 9% per year in carry. It is the market charging the price of fiscal risk in the interest rate, not in the exchange rate. That leaves the question that matters. Is this premium a cyclical discount for fiscal credibility, one that a convincing consolidation would return as appreciation, or is it a structural repricing of how much the world accepts paying to carry reais? The double-digit carry is the market's provisional answer to that question. Until it is resolved, the stagnant nominal exchange rate will keep hiding the fact that Brazil risk has not disappeared. It has simply changed instruments, from the spot exchange rate to the interest rate.

Sources and Method

USD/BRL, DXY, MSCI EM Currency Index, five-year CDS for Brazil and emerging-market peers: Investing.com, daily closing prices. IPCA: series 433, Central Bank of Brazil. CPI: series CPIAUCNS, FRED. Fed Funds: series FEDFUNDS, FRED. Selic: Copom calendar. Trade balance: series 22707, Central Bank of Brazil.

Fiscal risk and risk premium references: general government gross debt at 82.5% of GDP in July 2026 (BCB, DBGG series); IMF, Article IV Consultation for Brazil, July 2026, which uses a broader definition and projects 97.8% of GDP in 2026, heading toward about 106% by 2035 absent adjustment; Selic at 13.75% after the September 2026 Copom meeting (BCB); real interest rate ranking, InfoMoney, September 2026; market reading on fiscal policy and the exchange rate, Commerzbank, September 2026.

Window from September 2022 to September 2026, base exchange rate at 5.17. Parity: base-period dollar adjusted by the ratio between IPCA and CPI. Decomposition via a factor model on log returns, Newey-West errors, scenarios with 95% intervals via block bootstrap; robustness check on a rolling window from 2013 to 2026. Own calculations, auditable calculation record available in the supporting spreadsheet. Analytical text, not investment advice.
